## Union growth and decline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Union growth and decline")]

In the mid-1950s, 36% of the United States labor force was unionized. At America's union peak in the 1950s, union membership was lower in the United States than in most comparable countries. By 1989, that figure had dropped to about 16%, the lowest percentage of any developed democracy, except [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"). Union membership for other developed democracies, in 1986/87 were:[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-wsj-3)

*   95% in [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden") and [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark").
*   85% in [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland")
*   Over 60% in [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway") and [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria")
*   Over 50% in [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") and the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom").
*   Over 40% in [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy").
*   Over 30% in [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany").

In 1987, United States unionization was 37 points below the average of seventeen countries surveyed, down from 17 points below average in 1970.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-wsj-3) Between 1970 and 1987, union membership declined in only three other countries: Austria, by 3%, [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), by 7%, and the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), by 4%. In the United States, union membership had declined by 14%.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-4)

In 2008, 12.4% of U.S. wage and salary workers were union members. 36.8% of public sector workers were union members, but only 7.6% of workers in private sector industries were.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-5) The most unionized sectors of the economy have had the greatest decline in union membership. From 1953 to the late 1980s membership in construction fell from 84% to 22%, manufacturing from 42% to 25%, mining from 65% to 15%, and transportation from 80% to 37%.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-7)

From 1971 to the late 1980s, there was a 10% drop in union membership in the U.S. public sector and a 42% drop in union membership in the U.S. private sector.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-8) For comparison, there was no drop in union membership in the private sector in Sweden. In other countries drops included: [[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Sexton-9)

*   2% in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"),
*   3% in Norway,
*   6% in West Germany,
*   7% in [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland"),
*   9% in Austria,
*   14% in the United Kingdom,
*   15% in Italy.

Until the 1990s it was closely linked to the [French Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party") (PCF).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-10)

It is the largest in terms of votes (32.1% at the 2002 professional election, 34.0% in the 2008 election), and second largest in terms of membership numbers.

Its membership decreased to 650,000 members in 1995–96 (it had more than doubled when Socialist [François Mitterrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand "François Mitterrand") was elected President in 1981), before increasing today to between 700,000 and 720,000 members, slightly fewer than the [Confédération Française Démocratique du Travail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conf%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_Fran%C3%A7aise_D%C3%A9mocratique_du_Travail "Confédération Française Démocratique du Travail") (CFDT).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-11)

According to the historian M. Dreyfus, the direction of the CGT is slowly evolving, since the 1990s, during which it cut all organic links with the Communist Party, in favour of a more moderate stance. The CGT is concentrating its attention, in particular since the [1995 general strikes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_general_strikes_in_France "1995 general strikes in France"), to trade-unionism in the private sector.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-12)

#### CFTC/CFDT

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: CFTC/CFDT")]

The _[French Democratic Confederation of Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French\_Democratic\_Confederation\_of\_Labour "French Democratic Confederation of Labour")_, _CFDT_ is one of the five major confederations. It is the largest French trade union confederation by number of members (875,000) but comes only second after the [Confédération générale du travail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conf%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_du_travail "Confédération générale du travail") (CGT) in voting results for representative bodies.

The CFDT was created in 1964 when a majority of the members of the Christian trade union [Confédération Française des Travailleurs Chrétiens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conf%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_Fran%C3%A7aise_des_Travailleurs_Chr%C3%A9tiens "Confédération Française des Travailleurs Chrétiens") (CFTC) decided to become secular. The minority kept the name CFTC.

## Asia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Asia")]

### Japan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Japan")]

Main article: [Labor unions in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_unions_in_Japan "Labor unions in Japan")

Labour unions emerged in Japan in the second half of the [Meiji period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_period "Meiji period"), after 1890, as the country underwent a period of rapid industrialization.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Nimura-13) Until 1945, however, the labour movement remained weak, impeded by lack of legal rights,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Cross-14)[anti-union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-union "Anti-union") legislation,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Nimura-13) management-organized factory councils, and political divisions between “cooperative” and radical unionists.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Weathers-15) In the immediate aftermath of the Second World War, the [US Occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupation_of_Japan "Occupation of Japan") authorities initially encouraged the formation of independent unions.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Cross-14) Legislation was passed that enshrined the right to organize, and membership rapidly rose to 5 million by February 1947. The organization rate peaked at 55.8% of all workers in 1949[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-16) and subsequently declined to 18.5% as of 2010.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-jil.go.jp-17)

The labour movement went through a process of reorganization from 1987 to 1991[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-18) from which emerged the present configuration of three major labour union federations, along with other smaller national union organizations.

## North America

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: North America")]

### US and Canada

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: US and Canada")]

The unionization rate in the U.S. and Canada followed fairly similar paths from 1920 to the mid-1960s; both peaked at about 30%. However the U.S. rate declined steadily after 1974 to 12% in 2011. Meanwhile, the Canadian rate dropped from 37% the mid-1980s to 30% in 2010. Part of the reason is the different mixture of industry, and part is due to more favourable Canadian laws.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-19) In the United States, the [national trade union center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_trade_union_center "National trade union center") is the [AFL-CIO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL-CIO "AFL-CIO"), representing about 12.4 million workers,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-OLMS_LM-2_2020-09-28_AFL-CIO-20) while the [Canadian Labour Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Labour_Congress "Canadian Labour Congress") represents over 3 million Canadian workers.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-21) In Canada, the CLC is both historically and constitutionally affiliated with the [New Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democratic_Party "New Democratic Party")[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-22), while the AFL-CIO has no formal political affiliation.

In 1937 there were 4,740 strikes in the United States.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-23) This was the greatest strike wave in [American labor history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_history_of_the_United_States "Labor history of the United States"). The number of major strikes and lockouts in the U.S. fell by 97% from 381 in 1970 to 187 in 1980 to only 11 in 2010. Companies countered the threat of a strike by threatening to close or move a plant.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-census-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-25)

### Costa Rica

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Costa Rica")]

[![Image 43](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Agricultores%2C_manifestaci%C3%B3n_San_Jos%C3%A9_Costa_Rica%2C_enero_2011.jpg/250px-Agricultores%2C_manifestaci%C3%B3n_San_Jos%C3%A9_Costa_Rica%2C_enero_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Agricultores,_manifestaci%C3%B3n_San_Jos%C3%A9_Costa_Rica,_enero_2011.jpg)

Costa Rican agricultural unions demonstration, January 2011

Main article: [Trade unions in Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_unions_in_Costa_Rica "Trade unions in Costa Rica")

Labor unions first developed in [Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica "Costa Rica") in the late 1880s.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-SITRAPEQUIA-26) The first unions were organized with the help of the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-rojas-27) By 1913, the first International Workers Day was celebrated and unions, supported in particular by the [Popular Vanguard Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Costa_Rica) "People's Vanguard Party (Costa Rica)"),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-rojas-27) pushed for [Alfredo González Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfredo_Gonz%C3%A1lez_Flores "Alfredo González Flores")' tax reforms. Unions grew in number and coverage. A major historical event for Costa Rican labor was the 1934 [United Fruit Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Fruit_Company "United Fruit Company"), a national strike involving more than 30 unions which ended with many labor leaders imprisoned.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-rojas-27) Head of state [Teodoro Picado Michalski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teodoro_Picado_Michalski "Teodoro Picado Michalski") violently repressed union leaders, leading to the tensions that created the 1948 [Costa Rican Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rican_Civil_War "Costa Rican Civil War").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-rojas-27) Labor unions continued to grow, supported by the Catholic church, and the first [collective bargaining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_bargaining "Collective bargaining") agreement was reached in 1967. [Óscar Arias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%93scar_Arias "Óscar Arias") fought fiercely to dissolve and reduce the power of private sector unions in the 1980s.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-SECTOR_PRIVADO_COSTARRICENSE-28) Arias' austerity measures led to a period of increased labor activity as poverty and unemployment increased.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-hidalgo-29) Despite the resurgence, unions, particularly in the private sector, still faced opposition and repression.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Valverde-30) During the 2007 [Central American Free Trade Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_American_Free_Trade_Agreement "Central American Free Trade Agreement")[referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rican_Dominican_Republic_%E2%80%93_Central_America_Free_Trade_Agreement_referendum,_2007 "Costa Rican Dominican Republic – Central America Free Trade Agreement referendum, 2007"), labor unions unsuccessfully organized to encourage its rejection. [[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-haglund-31) They received a boost in political influence when [Luis Guillermo Solís](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs "Luis Guillermo Solís") and his [Citizens' Action Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizens'_Action_Party_(Costa_Rica) "Citizens' Action Party (Costa Rica)") earned the Presidency and several seats in the [Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Assembly_of_Costa_Rica "Legislative Assembly of Costa Rica").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-optimism-32)

Labor unions are active in both the public and private sectors. Major concerns include salaries increased to reflect [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation "Inflation"), regulation of public commodities, and a stronger [Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caja_Costarricense_del_Seguro_Social "Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social") (Costa Rican Social Security Department). Many labor unions are also asking for increased environmental regulation,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-optimism-32) and increased oversight of cooperative banks.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-avala-33) One important issue for Costa Rica unions is passage a new labor law.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-cambios-34) Former president [Laura Chinchilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Chinchilla "Laura Chinchilla") vetoed it, but Solís appears to want the issue passed, as do many members of the Legislative Assembly.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-avala-33)

## Violence in labor disputes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Violence in labor disputes")]

Between 1877 and 1968, 700 people have been killed in American labor disputes.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-36) In the 1890s, roughly two American workers were killed and 140 injured for every 100,000 strikers. In France, three French workers were injured for every 100,000 strikers. In the 1890s, only 70 French strikers were arrested per 100,000. For the United States, national arrest rates are simply impossible to compile. In Illinois, the arrest rate for the latter half of the 1890s decade was at least 700 per 100,000 strikers, or ten times that of France; in New York for that decade it was at least 400.

Between 1902 and 1904 in America , at least 198 people were killed, 1,966 workers were injured. One worker was killed and 1,009 were injured for every 100,000 strikers.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-38) Between 1877 and 1968, American state and federal troops intervened in labor disputes more than 160 times, almost invariably on behalf of employers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Sexton-9) Business was disrupted, usually by strikes, on 22,793 occasions between 1875 and 1900.

Other examples of the violence both by and against U.S. union members in the late 19th and early 20th centuries include the [Centralia Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centralia_Massacre_(Washington) "Centralia Massacre (Washington)"), the [Great Railroad Strike of 1922](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Railroad_Strike_of_1922 "Great Railroad Strike of 1922"), and the [Copper Country Strike of 1913-1914](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_Country_Strike_of_1913-1914 "Copper Country Strike of 1913-1914")

## Union growth and decline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Union growth and decline")]

In the mid-1950s, 36% of the United States labor force was unionized. At America's union peak in the 1950s, union membership was lower in the United States than in most comparable countries. By 1989, that figure had dropped to about 16%, the lowest percentage of any developed democracy, except [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"). Union membership for other developed democracies, in 1986/87 were:[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-wsj-3)

*   95% in [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden") and [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark").
*   85% in [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland")
*   Over 60% in [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway") and [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria")
*   Over 50% in [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") and the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom").
*   Over 40% in [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy").
*   Over 30% in [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany").

In 1987, United States unionization was 37 points below the average of seventeen countries surveyed, down from 17 points below average in 1970.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-wsj-3) Between 1970 and 1987, union membership declined in only three other countries: Austria, by 3%, [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), by 7%, and the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), by 4%. In the United States, union membership had declined by 14%.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-4)

In 2008, 12.4% of U.S. wage and salary workers were union members. 36.8% of public sector workers were union members, but only 7.6% of workers in private sector industries were.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-5) The most unionized sectors of the economy have had the greatest decline in union membership. From 1953 to the late 1980s membership in construction fell from 84% to 22%, manufacturing from 42% to 25%, mining from 65% to 15%, and transportation from 80% to 37%.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-7)

From 1971 to the late 1980s, there was a 10% drop in union membership in the U.S. public sector and a 42% drop in union membership in the U.S. private sector.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-8) For comparison, there was no drop in union membership in the private sector in Sweden. In other countries drops included: [[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Sexton-9)

*   2% in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"),
*   3% in Norway,
*   6% in West Germany,
*   7% in [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland"),
*   9% in Austria,
*   14% in the United Kingdom,
*   15% in Italy.

The [General Confederation of Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conf%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_G%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_du_Travail "Confédération Générale du Travail") (_CGT_) is a [national trade union center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_trade_union_center "National trade union center"), the first of the five major French confederations of trade unions. Until the 1990s it was closely linked to the [French Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party") (PCF).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-10)

It is the largest in terms of votes (32.1% at the 2002 professional election, 34.0% in the 2008 election), and second largest in terms of membership numbers.

Its membership decreased to 650,000 members in 1995–96 (it had more than doubled when Socialist [François Mitterrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand "François Mitterrand") was elected President in 1981), before increasing today to between 700,000 and 720,000 members, slightly fewer than the [Confédération Française Démocratique du Travail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conf%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_Fran%C3%A7aise_D%C3%A9mocratique_du_Travail "Confédération Française Démocratique du Travail") (CFDT).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-11)

According to the historian M. Dreyfus, the direction of the CGT is slowly evolving, since the 1990s, during which it cut all organic links with the Communist Party, in favour of a more moderate stance. The CGT is concentrating its attention, in particular since the [1995 general strikes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_general_strikes_in_France "1995 general strikes in France"), to trade-unionism in the private sector.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-12)

#### CFTC/CFDT

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: CFTC/CFDT")]

The _[French Democratic Confederation of Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French\_Democratic\_Confederation\_of\_Labour "French Democratic Confederation of Labour")_, _CFDT_ is one of the five major confederations. It is the largest French trade union confederation by number of members (875,000) but comes only second after the [Confédération générale du travail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conf%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_du_travail "Confédération générale du travail") (CGT) in voting results for representative bodies.

The CFDT was created in 1964 when a majority of the members of the Christian trade union [Confédération Française des Travailleurs Chrétiens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conf%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_Fran%C3%A7aise_des_Travailleurs_Chr%C3%A9tiens "Confédération Française des Travailleurs Chrétiens") (CFTC) decided to become secular. ## Asia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Asia")]

### Japan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Japan")]

Main article: [Labor unions in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_unions_in_Japan "Labor unions in Japan")

Labour unions emerged in Japan in the second half of the [Meiji period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_period "Meiji period"), after 1890, as the country underwent a period of rapid industrialization.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Nimura-13) Until 1945, however, the labour movement remained weak, impeded by lack of legal rights,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Cross-14)[anti-union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-union "Anti-union") legislation,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Nimura-13) management-organized factory councils, and political divisions between “cooperative” and radical unionists.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Weathers-15) In the immediate aftermath of the Second World War, the [US Occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupation_of_Japan "Occupation of Japan") authorities initially encouraged the formation of independent unions.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Cross-14) Legislation was passed that enshrined the right to organize, and membership rapidly rose to 5 million by February 1947. The organization rate peaked at 55.8% of all workers in 1949[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-16) and subsequently declined to 18.5% as of 2010.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-jil.go.jp-17)

The labour movement went through a process of reorganization from 1987 to 1991[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-18) from which emerged the present configuration of three major labour union federations, along with other smaller national union organizations.

## North America

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: North America")]

### US and Canada

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: US and Canada")]

The unionization rate in the U.S. and Canada followed fairly similar paths from 1920 to the mid-1960s; both peaked at about 30%. However the U.S. rate declined steadily after 1974 to 12% in 2011. Meanwhile, the Canadian rate dropped from 37% the mid-1980s to 30% in 2010. Part of the reason is the different mixture of industry, and part is due to more favourable Canadian laws.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-19) In the United States, the [national trade union center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_trade_union_center "National trade union center") is the [AFL-CIO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL-CIO "AFL-CIO"), representing about 12.4 million workers,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-OLMS_LM-2_2020-09-28_AFL-CIO-20) while the [Canadian Labour Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Labour_Congress "Canadian Labour Congress") represents over 3 million Canadian workers.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-21) In Canada, the CLC is both historically and constitutionally affiliated with the [New Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democratic_Party "New Democratic Party")[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-22), while the AFL-CIO has no formal political affiliation.

In 1937 there were 4,740 strikes in the United States.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-23) This was the greatest strike wave in [American labor history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_history_of_the_United_States "Labor history of the United States"). The number of major strikes and lockouts in the U.S. fell by 97% from 381 in 1970 to 187 in 1980 to only 11 in 2010. Companies countered the threat of a strike by threatening to close or move a plant.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-census-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-25)

### Costa Rica

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Costa Rica")]

[![Image 43](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Agricultores%2C_manifestaci%C3%B3n_San_Jos%C3%A9_Costa_Rica%2C_enero_2011.jpg/250px-Agricultores%2C_manifestaci%C3%B3n_San_Jos%C3%A9_Costa_Rica%2C_enero_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Agricultores,_manifestaci%C3%B3n_San_Jos%C3%A9_Costa_Rica,_enero_2011.jpg)

Costa Rican agricultural unions demonstration, January 2011

Main article: [Trade unions in Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_unions_in_Costa_Rica "Trade unions in Costa Rica")

Labor unions first developed in [Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica "Costa Rica") in the late 1880s.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-SITRAPEQUIA-26) The first unions were organized with the help of the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-rojas-27) By 1913, the first International Workers Day was celebrated and unions, supported in particular by the [Popular Vanguard Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Costa_Rica) "People's Vanguard Party (Costa Rica)"),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-rojas-27) pushed for [Alfredo González Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfredo_Gonz%C3%A1lez_Flores "Alfredo González Flores")' tax reforms. Unions grew in number and coverage. A major historical event for Costa Rican labor was the 1934 [United Fruit Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Fruit_Company "United Fruit Company"), a national strike involving more than 30 unions which ended with many labor leaders imprisoned.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-rojas-27) Head of state [Teodoro Picado Michalski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teodoro_Picado_Michalski "Teodoro Picado Michalski") violently repressed union leaders, leading to the tensions that created the 1948 [Costa Rican Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rican_Civil_War "Costa Rican Civil War").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-rojas-27) Labor unions continued to grow, supported by the Catholic church, and the first [collective bargaining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_bargaining "Collective bargaining") agreement was reached in 1967. [Óscar Arias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%93scar_Arias "Óscar Arias") fought fiercely to dissolve and reduce the power of private sector unions in the 1980s.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-SECTOR_PRIVADO_COSTARRICENSE-28) Arias' austerity measures led to a period of increased labor activity as poverty and unemployment increased.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-hidalgo-29) Despite the resurgence, unions, particularly in the private sector, still faced opposition and repression.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Valverde-30) During the 2007 [Central American Free Trade Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_American_Free_Trade_Agreement "Central American Free Trade Agreement")[referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rican_Dominican_Republic_%E2%80%93_Central_America_Free_Trade_Agreement_referendum,_2007 "Costa Rican Dominican Republic – Central America Free Trade Agreement referendum, 2007"), labor unions unsuccessfully organized to encourage its rejection. [[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-haglund-31) They received a boost in political influence when [Luis Guillermo Solís](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs "Luis Guillermo Solís") and his [Citizens' Action Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizens'_Action_Party_(Costa_Rica) "Citizens' Action Party (Costa Rica)") earned the Presidency and several seats in the [Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Assembly_of_Costa_Rica "Legislative Assembly of Costa Rica").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-optimism-32)

Labor unions are active in both the public and private sectors. Major concerns include salaries increased to reflect [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation "Inflation"), regulation of public commodities, and a stronger [Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caja_Costarricense_del_Seguro_Social "Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social") (Costa Rican Social Security Department). Many labor unions are also asking for increased environmental regulation,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-optimism-32) and increased oversight of cooperative banks.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-avala-33) One important issue for Costa Rica unions is passage a new labor law.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-cambios-34) Former president [Laura Chinchilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Chinchilla "Laura Chinchilla") vetoed it, but Solís appears to want the issue passed, as do many members of the Legislative Assembly.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-avala-33)

## Unemployment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Unemployment")]

## Violence in labor disputes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_comparisons_of_trade_unions&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Violence in labor disputes")]

Between 1877 and 1968, 700 people have been killed in American labor disputes.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-36) In the 1890s, roughly two American workers were killed and 140 injured for every 100,000 strikers. In France, three French workers were injured for every 100,000 strikers. In the 1890s, only 70 French strikers were arrested per 100,000. For the United States, national arrest rates are simply impossible to compile. In Illinois, the arrest rate for the latter half of the 1890s decade was at least 700 per 100,000 strikers, or ten times that of France; in New York for that decade it was at least 400.

Between 1902 and 1904 in America , at least 198 people were killed, 1,966 workers were injured. One worker was killed and 1,009 were injured for every 100,000 strikers.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-38) Between 1877 and 1968, American state and federal troops intervened in labor disputes more than 160 times, almost invariably on behalf of employers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Sexton-9) Business was disrupted, usually by strikes, on 22,793 occasions between 1875 and 1900.

Other examples of the violence both by and against U.S. union members in the late 19th and early 20th centuries include the [Centralia Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centralia_Massacre_(Washington) "Centralia Massacre (Washington)"), the [Great Railroad Strike of 1922](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Railroad_Strike_of_1922 "Great Railroad Strike of 1922"), and the [Copper Country Strike of 1913-1914](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_Country_Strike_of_1913-1914 "Copper Country Strike of 1913-1914")

ביום 30.11.2021 פורסמו להערות ציבור 12 טיוטות מפרטים אחידים. את הערות הציבור ניתן להגיש עד ליום 30.1.2022. למידע נוסף ראו באיזור "טיוטות מפרטים אחידים להערות הציבור". |  
ביום 24.11.2021 פרסם המשרד להגנת הסביבה הצעה לשינוי במפרט האחיד של פריט 3.2א' (בעלי חיים, לרבות ימיים | בעלי חיים, למעט עופות – גידולם, אחזקתם, טיפול בהם), להערות הציבור. ניתן להעביר הערות עד ליום 26.12.2021. למידע נוסף ראו באתר המשרד להגנת הסביבה ß שיתוף ציבור – הערות הציבור ß הצעה לשינוי מפרט אחיד לפריט רישוי 3.2א בצו רישוי עסקים (עסקים טעוני רישוי), התשע"ג-2013.
